As we enter the final stretch of 2025 and prepare to embark on a new
year, I am pleased to introduce the Single Programming Document
(SPD) 2026-2028 which outlines our roadmap for the next three years.
Building on the revised strategy and organisational changes
introduced last year, we are focussed on delivering on our core tasks
and realising key business developments to respond to the needs of
our Industry, while driving efficiency through simplification and
digitalisation of our activities.
Safety is our core business. As the aviation sector continues to navigate a complex and dynamic landscape,
marked by geopolitical tensions, rapid technological innovation, shifting consumer expectations, and a growing
emphasis on sustainability and environmental protection, it is more important than ever that we stay focussed
on our core principles. We will continue to promote a safe, secure, and sustainable aviation system that
benefits all European citizens whilst also leveraging our expertise and experience to address the emerging
challenges and opportunities that are shaping the future of aviation. These include the integration of new
technologies such as unmanned aircraft systems and artificial intelligence, leveraging safety data capabilities
to better assess and mitigate safety risks, and facilitating the introduction of green technologies and
sustainable fuels.
To address those challenges, we must also continue to prioritise the creation of efficiencies throughout our
organisation and maintain a disciplined approach to financial management. Digitalisation will play a critical
role in our journey towards efficiency and sustainability. We must continue to invest in tools and reimagine
processes that enable us to work smarter, faster, and more effectively. By embracing digital transformation,
we will unlock new opportunities to improve our services to stakeholders and ultimately make the best use of
our human and financial resources.
As we look to the future, we must also consider the generational shift brought about by the changing
demographics of our workforce. The onboarding of newcomers brings new ideas, new perspectives, and
energy to our organisation. At the same time, we are cautious not to lose the wealth of knowledge and
expertise of those colleagues who helped to build and shape EASA into the organisation it is today. We need
to be able to attract and retain new talent, preserve institutional memory and build a workforce that is fit for
the future, equipped with the skills and competences necessary to drive success into the next decade, in an
environment that is inclusive, supportive, and empowering.
I am very excited about the new opportunities and challenges that lie ahead for EASA, and I would like to thank
our staff, EU institutions, stakeholders, and partners for their hard work and support. I look forward to
continuing working together to deliver our mandate and achieve our goals.
1st October 2025
Florian GUILLERMET
EASA Executive Director

1. Introduction
The aviation sector is navigating a complex landscape of global trends driven by shifting politics, economic
fluctuations, evolving societal norms, rapid technological advancements and growing environmental concerns.
The unprecedented challenges over the last 5 years have demonstrated the resilience of the sector with air
traffic forecasted to return to 2019 levels by 2026, growing moderately up to 2030 (Eurocontrol 7-year Forecast
for Europe 2024-2030 (autumn update 2024).
As the sector looks to the future, two key trends are emerging: the rapid growth of aviation outside of Europe,
and the accelerating adoption of innovative products and digital technologies, including artificial intelligence
and advanced information technologies. These trends present both opportunities and challenges, from
ensuring the safe integration of new technologies and preserving high safety standards, to addressing the
climate challenge and promoting sustainable aviation practices.
Against this backdrop, EASA continues to evolve to meet the changing needs of its stakeholders. With a
mandate that has expanded since its inception in 2002, EASA is playing a critical role in setting and promoting
safety standards, providing oversight, and enabling the development of innovative solutions that enhance
competitiveness, environmental sustainability, and digitalisation. As a regulator, EASA is committed to
supporting the European industry's growth, innovation, and competitiveness, while ensuring the highest
standards of safety and environmental protection.

2. European Plan for Aviation Safety (EPAS)
The European Plan for Aviation Safety (EPAS) is a key component of the European aviation safety system. The
main objective of EPAS is to further improve aviation safety and environmental protection throughout Europe,
while ensuring a level playing field, as well as efficiency/proportionality in regulatory processes. EPAS
constitutes a common aviation safety plan for EASA and the Member States, setting out the strategic priorities
and main risks affecting the European aviation safety system and the necessary actions to mitigate those risks
and to further improve aviation safety.
The strategic priorities for the EPAS underwent a light review in 2025, aligning medium-term goals with the
highest risk areas and available resources in the Single Programming Document (SPD). It is anticipated that a
completely revised EPAS will be published in 2027.
Further information can be found on EASA’s Website: European Plan for Aviation Safety | EASA

the EC priorities constitute key references for EASA in defining its strategy, priorities and business

Climate Policy
The EU climate policy is one of the most ambitious attempts worldwide to address risks related to the climate
change, air quality, and noise. By 2030 the Zero Pollution Action Plan aims to reduce pollution at source,
including the reduction of the share of people chronically disturbed by transport noise by 30% and improve air
quality to reduce the number of premature deaths caused by air pollution by 55%, compared to 2017 levels.
The Environmental Noise Directive and the Balanced Approach Regulation aim to reduce noise exposure in
cities and near major transport infrastructure.
On climate change, the 2021 Climate Law incorporated Green Deal targets into EU law, namely climate
neutrality by 2050 and a 2030 target of at least a 55% reduction in net emissions of greenhouse gases as
compared to 1990. In 2024 the recommended target for 2040 was set at a 90% reduction compared to 1990.
In the transport sector this target has been translated into a goal to reduce
emissions by 90% in 2050 compared to 1990 levels.

On 6 February 2024, the European Parliament and the Council reached a political agreement on the Net-Zero
Industry Act. This initiative from the Green Deal Industrial Plan aims to scale up the manufacturing of
technologies in the EU that support the clean energy transition by simplifying the regulatory framework and
increasing the competitiveness of European industry.
For further information see II. Multi-Annual Programming – “Green” strategic goals and priorities and III.3.1. Sustainable

Sustainable and Smart Mobility Strategy
By 2030 the EU expects 100 European cities to be climate neutral,
scheduled collective travel for journeys under 500 km to be carbon neutral,
and automated mobility to be deployed at large scale. By 2035 it further
expects zero-emission large aircraft to be market-ready. This means:
#1 Boosting the uptake of zero-emission vehicles, vessels and aeroplanes, renewable & low-carbon fuels and
related infrastructure.
#2 Creating zero-emission airports and ports – for instance through new initiatives to promote sustainable aviation
and maritime fuels.
#3 Making interurban and urban mobility healthy and sustainable.
#4 Greening freight transport.
#5 Pricing carbon and providing better incentives for users – for instance by pursuing a comprehensive set of
measures to deliver fair and efficient pricing across all transport.
#6 Making connected and automated multimodal mobility a reality.
#7 Boosting innovation and the use of data and artificial intelligence (AI) for smarter mobility – for instance by fully
supporting the deployment of drones and unmanned aircraft and further actions to build a European Common
Mobility Data Space.
#8 Reinforcing the Single Market – for instance through reinforcing efforts and investments to complete the Trans-
European Transport Network (TEN-T) by 2030 and support the sector to build back better through increased
investments, both public and private, in the modernisation of fleets in all modes.
#9 Making mobility fair and just for all.
#10 Ste pping up transport safety and security across all modes – including by bringing the death toll close to zero by
2050.
For further information see II. Multi-Annual Programming – “Safe”, “Green” & “Innovative” strategic goals and priorities.
Drones Strategy 2.0
By 2030 the EU expects emergency services, mapping, imaging, inspection and surveillance to be undertaken
by civil drones, as well as the urgent delivery of small consignments, such as biological samples or medicines.
It also expects Innovative Air Mobility services, such as air taxis, to be providing regular transport services for
passengers, initially with a pilot on board, but with the ultimate aim of fully automating operations. This means:
#1 Adopting common rules for airworthiness, and new training requirements for remote and eVTOL (manned
electric Vertical Take Off and Landing) aircraft pilots.
#2 Funding the creation of an online platform to support local stakeholders and industry in implementing
sustainable Innovative Air Mobility.
#3 Developing a Strategic Drone Technology Roadmap to identify priority areas for research and innovation, to
reduce existing strategic dependencies and avoid new ones arising.
#4 Defining criteria for a voluntary cybersecurity-approved drone label.

Green
EASA has had a mandate to protect the environment and public health since its foundation,
with an aim to ensure the highest environmental protection standards in product
certification. This is done through ensuring that the applicable aircraft noise and emissions
standards are complied with as part of the type certification process. In addition, EASA
environmental experts drive the further development of state-of-the-art environmental
protection standards at European and international levels, including but not limited to CO2
and non-CO2 emissions.
EASA is facilitating the market entry of reduced emission propulsion technologies such as electric, hybrid and
hydrogen systems, and novel architectures (e.g. open rotor) to support the aviation s ’s ms reduce
aircraft noise and emissions across all aircraft product categories. With the entry into force of the ReFuelEU
Aviation regulation the EASA mandate in emissions reduction has been extended. The priorities are to deliver
on commitments to the uptake of SAF, couple environmental protection with consistently high levels of safety,
and attract young talent with the right mixture of technical competence and environmental awareness.
The Agency aims to address the following 3 key strategic goals (SG):
SG08 The transition to sustainable aviation fuels (SAF) as a major fuel source for aviation is safe and sustainable and
its uptake by EU operators is reliably monitored and reported.
SG09 The environmental performance of the commercial operations can be demonstrated through clear and
transparent reporting and labelling.
SG10 The safety and environmental requirements for the design and operation of aircraft, including clean
propulsion technologies, are clear and permit timely entry into service.

The Basic Regulation establishes the need to support the competitiveness of European
industry in the global market. This competitiveness is spearheaded by innovation in the
sector, which is accelerating and diversifying rapidly. Industrial technology development is
also a key factor in driving the digital and green transitions.
The Single Basic Act reinforces the role of EASA in research and innovation, giving it a specific
role to guide viable research initiatives such as the EU public-private partnerships of Clean
Aviation and SESAR 3 through to the stages of certification and operation.
The Agency aims to address the following 2 key strategic goals (SG):
SG11 New technologies and market developments are safely and efficiently integrated into aviation and non-
aviation systems and are effectively overseen.
SG12 The European aerospace industry can count on strong support to facilitate innovation and the effective
commercial uptake of new technologies.

The Agency is central to the hub-and-spoke architecture of the European regional safety
oversight system. It must remain resilient to both normal and abnormal operating conditions,
otherwise the system will be weakened. Resilience requires a common sense of purpose and
a focus on good processes – for that the Agency staff members should feel informed, engaged
and proud to be part of an organisation that works to common goals.
To effectively meet stakeholder needs the Basic Regulation empowers the Executive Director
to adapt the processes, organisation and resources of the Agency to changing needs. In the current context
the Agency aims to address the following 4 key strategic goals (SG) to ensure that:
SG13 Agency staff has a common sense of purpose, governance structures are clear, and processes are well
designed, digitalised, and consistently applied.
SG14 Revenue and expenditure are sustainably balanced and transparently managed.
SG15 Digital processes and physical infrastructure enable operational efficiency, agility and strategic growth in a
secure, sustainable environment.
SG16 Staff are supported to maintain their credibility through technical excellence, and corporate knowledge is
retained and keeps pace with industrial technology developments.

growing volume and complexity of workload, compounded by high inflation rates, which have accelerated the
urgency for actions to ensure the financial sustainability of the Agency.

3.2. Outlook for 2026-2028
The workload for the Agency is forecasted to continue grow over the next years. Most notably:
Growing F&C Market Driven Workload: Sustained high workload for certification and
organisation approval domains with further increases forecasted in particular under Initial
Airworthiness (IAW), Design Organisation Approval (DOA) and Production Organisation Approval
(POA). Moreover, the growing complexity and novelty of applications from emerging domains
and innovative technology, such as the application for U-space Service Providers certification,
continue to stretch the existing capacity and reinforce the need for safeguarding competency in
both traditional and emerging domains. EASA works closely with National Competent Authority
Partners (NCAs) to manage the evolving F&C workload demand, however, those applications

Establishment of new domains for ATM/ANS: The most critical workload evolution forecasted
for the period 2025-2028 is within the framework of the ATM/ANS equipment certification and
approval of Design and Production Organisations (DPO). EASA has already started receiving
applications in 2025 and is anticipating a swift ramp-up in applications over the coming years.
EASA is already working with NCAs to manage this increase in workload, whereby like EASA,
capacity and knowledge will need to be built progressively. Nevertheless, the workload that
EASA is not be able to accommodate during the ramp-up phase will be placed “G w ”.
Enabling Mandatory Regulatory & Strategic Developments to support Industrial
Competitiveness: The Agency continues to mobilise resources to support the European aviation
industry by preparing the regulatory framework to accommodate innovations. Key priorities
include drones, clean propulsion technologies, sustainable aviation fuels, ATM/ANS
technologies being deployed through the ATM Master Plan and the CNS Evolution Plan,
developments under the SES2+ regulation, dual use (civil/military) equipment, new simulator
technologies, and changes associated with the broader digitalisation of aviation, such as the
increased risk of hacking, spoofing and jamming.
Technical Compliance & Quality Assurance: In light of increased compliance requirements such
as cybersecurity including Part-IS, increased responsibilities from emerging domains such as Art.
64/65 and ATM/ANS conformity assessment, increased use of external partners to offset high
workload, and high scrutiny from external stakeholders and oversight bodies/audit entities such
as IAS, it is more important than ever that EASA is able to maintain the high technical quality and
compliance of its work and the work outsourced to its partners.

Process Improvements
The benefits of the recently streamlined rulemaking process are beginning to emerge. Further
smart adjustments to the organisational structure and process responsibilities will optimise synergy

At system level, EASA has a role to play in supporting the harmonised implementation of the European

The sharing of resources internally between teams is an integral practice at EASA, allowing for sharing of
knowledge and expertise as well as providing temporary capacity to fill resource bottlenecks and/or peak work

Approving safe market access.
As competent authority, EASA certifies the airworthiness of products, parts, and appliances for
access to the Single Market. It complements the certification of products with the approval of the organisations
responsible for the design, production, maintenance and repair of the products, and the organisations
responsible for the competence of associated personnel. In addition, EASA also assesses the safety of third
country operators intending to operate in the Single Market. Moreover, it is important for the persistent safety
of the system are the continued airworthiness and organisational surveillance activities that ensure continuing
industry compliance with prevailing standards. This centralisation greatly simplifies the European aviation
safety system for regulators and industry alike, ensuring efficiency and expertise.
2.1. Certification
EASA is responsible for the airworthiness and the environmental protection certification of aeronautical
products and parts. This responsibility encompasses the initial type certification (IAW), including operational
suitability data and a variety of related certification activities, such as supplemental type certifications,
approval of changes to type certificate and of repair designs. All these activities are performed to maintain the
highest level of safety and environmental compatibility. It also covers activities to ensure the continuing
airworthiness (CAW) of the certified products and parts throughout their entire operational life. This includes
identifying and reacting without undue delay to unsafe conditions and issuing and disseminating the applicable
mandatory Airworthiness Directives (ADs).
In addition, the Agency will conduct investigations, audits and other monitoring activities necessary for the
certification and declaration of air traffic management/air navigation services systems and constituents and
ensure an effective oversight.
EASA also provides certification support for EU industry for validation of certificates (CSV) outside the EASA
member states, including through the development and implementation of streamlined procedures with
bilateral partners. Likewise, services to external stakeholders, such as the approval of maintenance review
board reports, technical advice contracts, pre-application contracts and innovation partnership contracts can
be provided upon request of either the industry, aviation authorities or other public institutions.

2.5. EU Ramp Inspection Programme
The EU Ramp Inspection Programme is a European programme regarding the performance of ramp
inspections on aircraft used by Third Country Operators (Safety Assessment of Foreign Aircraft (SAFA)
inspections) or used by operators under the regulatory oversight of another EU Member State (Safety
Assessment of Community Aircraft (SACA) inspections).
The Programme is regulated in detail by Commission Regulation (EU) 965/2012. Although any aircraft, used by
third country operators or used by operators under the regulatory oversight of another Member State when
landed at aerodromes located in the territory subject to the provisions of the Treaty, may be subject to a ramp
inspection, the focus is on those aircraft identified as presenting a potential risk, including those suspected of
non-compliance with the applicable requirements (based on e.g. safety-relevant information collected by the
Participating States or based on regular analysis of the centralised database performed by EASA).

2.8. Safety Intelligence & Performance
The Agency's safety intelligence and performance process serves as a central hub for consolidating
and assessing different streams and sources of safety data. Through converging these analysis streams, EASA
can comprehensively assess safety issues, identify potential risks, and determine whether such risks are
isolated or part of a broader systemic issue (e.g. cross organisation, cross domain, recurrent incidents, patterns
of non-compliance etc.). Issues not classified s “s s m ” m d d spective EASA core
activities such as certification, organisation
approval, etc.
The identification of systemic issues is part of the
’s S R sk M m (SRM) P ss,
enabling an in-depth assessment of the issue. The
SRM also defines the targeted intervention
actions, proportionate to the risk to ensure a swift
and effective mitigation response. The relevant
outputs are an important element of the
European Plan for Aviation Safety (EPAS).
Safety intelligence relies on the collection,
processing and analysis of all relevant safety data and information. Relevant data are, amongst others, safety
occurrence reports, flight data generated by the aircraft, air traffic data, and weather data. EASA works
extensively with safety partners, such as industry stakeholders and National Competent Authorities (NCAs) to
enable sharing of information, research, competence, to enhance analysis capabilities.
Internally, EASA has developed a network of work steams to facilitate the process, leveraging data collection,
analysis capabilities and or means to effect change. Some of the notable elements are:
ꟷ Data4Safety (D4S): Large-scale collaborative data collection and analysis programme aiming to
significantly increase the aviation safety intelligence capacity in Europe, leveraging data analytics and
artificial intelligence (AI) to identify and manage potential safety risks and trends.
Launched in 2017, D4S is now approaching a critical operational phase and has already enabled the EU
MS and Industry to join forces and team-up to work together for safety on a scale not so far seen in
European aviation.
ꟷ ECCAIRS: Develop, maintain and operate the European Central Repository (ECR) to support the
implementation of the occurrence reporting and processing procedures of industry and Member
States, linked with D4S programme to enable analytics and safety intelligence based on ECR data.
ꟷ Safety Data Management: Coding and analysis of technical occurrences reported to EASA in its role as
a competent authority. Data is shared with ECR and occurrences grouped to facilitate monitoring and
long-term analysis by technical owners.
ꟷ Confidential Safety Reporting (CSR): Processing of reports made to EASA (on a voluntary basis) of
alleged malpractices and irregularities in the field of aviation safety. System allows reporting without
the reporter having to fear that their action may have adverse consequences for their person.
I
55

Important complement to safety intelligence as can lead to effective detection and follow-up of
breaches, irregularities, and malpractices of the EU aviation safety legal framework that otherwise
might remain hidden and could cause serious harm to aviation safety.
ꟷ Accident Investigations & Safety Recommendations: EASA participates to investigations of serious
incidents and accidents, to capitalise on the lessons learned and apply relevant corrective actions.
ꟷ Cybersecurity in Aviation: EASA works closely with partners to share information, research and
competence to assess risks and develop industry standards. Provides an important source of data for
assessing emerging risks and cyber threats.
ꟷ Conflict Zones (CZ): EASA supports the EU CZ Alerting Mechanism, where MS exchange information

3. Strategic Initiatives & Activities
To enable regulatory & strategic developments in support of industrial competitiveness EASA invests in
research, innovation actions and strategic projects on selected topics which allows EASA to advise competently
on emerging risks and measures to mitigate them as well as prepare for the future accordingly.
Foreseeing and shaping future opportunities.
To this end, EASA creates transversal projects, across organisation units / activities, to make use of
the broad spectrum of expertise in-house, as well as leveraging external resources when required, to
consolidate efforts at corporate level, maximise success and optimise the use of resources.
3.1. Sustainable Aviation
S ’s m d s s w ds v m l v l safety and environmental
protection in the field of aviation. This includes reducing noise, improving air quality and mitigating climate
change. In cooperation with global partners and industry, the Agency strives for a cleaner, quieter, and more
sustainable aviation system. O S ’s s bj v s s b ’s l b m

emissions by at least 55% by 2030and put Europe on a responsible path to becoming climate neutral by 2050.
In 2023, EASA’s v m l m d w s x d d under the RefuelEU Aviation regulation (Regulation
(EU) 2023/2405) which promotes the increased use of sustainable aviation fuels (SAF) as the single most
powerful tool to decrease aviation CO emissions. It sets requirements for aviation fuel suppliers to gradually

increase the share of SAF blended into the conventional aviation fuel supplied at EU airports. S ’s w

associated emission reductions in the EU airports. I 2024, “S s bility Portal” was launched to
facilitate the reporting exercise to AOs and the National Competent Authorities (NCAs).
ꟷ Art. 13: Publication of an annual report stating the regulation compliance status, the SAF and fuel
supplied, characteristics and other relevant information. 2025 will serve as a test year for the reporting,
with the publication of a technical report using with the data of 2024 (dry run). The official RefuelEU
Aviation reporting obligations will start in 2026 with the data of 2025.

(FEL) aims at providing consumers with clear, accurate and standardised information about the
environmental performance of the flights they book. On 31st December 2024 the FEL Implement
Regulation was published in the Official Journal and a new contribution agreement in 2025 will develop

3.3. Innovative Air Mobility
The safe, secure and sustainable integration of civil drones, air taxis and higher airspace aircraft and operations
into European airspace, without compromising safety, security or disrupting current operations, is critical to
facilitate the competitiveness of the aviation industry.
Initiated in 2016, the Innovative Air Mobility programme (former Drones Programme) aims to establish a risk
based, operation centric EU regulatory framework for Unmanned Aircraft Systems (UAS) forming the basis for
mm d s d s’ m k , d bl m l l s BVLOS S s
by implementing the U-space framework. This innovative field requires upstream engagement with
stakeholders to allow these new technologies, operations and business models to enter the market through a
timely and proportionate regulatory approach.
I 2022 C bl s d “EU Drone Strategy 2.0 for a Smart and Sustainable Unmanned Aircraft Eco-
S s m ” w S s k b mb l s s.
The programme has already achieved some key milestones through publication of a first set of EU UAS and U-
space regulations and the publication of the first EU Regulations for UAS in the certified category and manned
VTOL capable aircraft operations to enable first IAM operations. The Agency has also started standardisation
activities of Member States and has taking up its role as Authority for the certification of U-space Service
Providers (USSP), as well as a range of promotion and internal cooperation activities.
For further information please visit the EASA Website: Civil drones (unmanned aircraft) | EASA (europa.eu)
Initiated in 2020, the work on Higher Airspace Operations, led by a Task Force of Member States together with
EASA, delivered a Proposed Roadmap on Higher Airspace Operations in March 2023, as an initial exploration
of the regulatory challenges around these operations, which can be manned or unmanned. The Roadmap
which recommended further preparatory actions was endorsed by the European Commission, who
recommended EASA to implement the proposed actions and to be closely involved in the SESAR JU ECHO
project. Furthermore, the European Parliament (TRAN) has proposed a Preparatory Action aimed at supporting
the development of a regulatory framework for HAO in Europe.
In the coming years the project aims to address the following 3 key objectives: 1)Draft the EU regulatory
framework for HAO by end-2027; 2) Develop guidance material on regulatory sandboxes to facilitate industry
tests and demonstrations in the EU & 3) Influence global regulatory developments at ICAO level.

3.4. Future Connectivity
On 9 November 2022, EASA, the FAA, Airbus and Boeing (EU/US Task Force - TF) published a White
Paper on Future Connectivity for Aviation, followed by two identical public webinars on 19 January and 1
February 2023. The initiative aimed at rethinking aviation connectivity and defining a blueprint for the
modernisation and harmonisation of the aviation data communication landscape by 2035.
Aviation connectivity supports the various air-ground data exchanges that are becoming increasingly essential
to support safe, sustainable and efficient ATM and the air operations of tomorrow. It is currently supported by
a set of technologies that rely to a large extent on VHF datalink and on first generation aviation SATCOM
connectivity. While these technologies have served the aviation community well for decades, they are in need
for upgrade and for more harmonisation.
The jointly proposed vision for the future aviation connectivity landscape is based on the combination of
aviation specific solutions (VHF datalink and higher performance L-band SATCOM) – that will offer guaranteed
safety and performance – with commercial, non-aviation specific solutions (hyperconnected ATM) – that are
expected to provide for high capacity and economic efficiency.

3.5. Research & Innovation
EASA supports the competitiveness of the aviation industry by ensuring that regulations are
proportionate to risks, eliminating barriers to innovation, closing gaps in the regulatory framework and by
fostering a level playing field across the sector. An active engagement in Research and Innovation (R&I)
projects is critical to anticipate future regulatory needs and to ensure industrial competitiveness.
With the rapid pace of technological advancement, EASA needs to be involved from the early stages of
innovation, supporting the integration of new technologies, services, operations and business models into the
European aviation system, without compromising on safety or becoming a bottleneck to progress. By
prioritizing upstream involvement in R&I and steering the EU R&I agenda in civil aviation in cooperation with
the European Commission, the Member States, and the research community, EASA develops a robust
regulatory framework and sound certification and oversight policies that enable the rapid uptake of new
technologies and business models as soon as they are technically mature. These enable the swift adoption of
mature technologies while maintaining safety and sustainability. The key to achieve this is a strategic foresight
approach, requiring the consistent engagement of EASA experts in projects in the research and innovation
pipeline. This allows early identification of risks and the development of mitigation strategies.
As technologically advanced products operate within complex system environments, and to ensure that a
system-wide safety assessment and integrated risk management (in a manner that respects the nature,
sensitivity (need to know), protection levels, and specificities of the domains concerned) can be performed,
the concept of operations (CONOPS) is essential. This requires a total system view of upcoming changes and
to anticipate new emerging risks by an active involvement in testing and demonstrators of innovative solutions.
Regulatory sandboxes enabling the testing of new products, systems, technologies in a controlled real-world
environment need to be put in place to identify gaps and barriers in existing regulations or, when there is no
regulatory framework, to have the possibility to provide an experimental regulatory environment to safeguard
safety and sustainability and learn about the opportunities and risks that a particular innovation carries. A close
partnership with the Member States is vital to establish regulatory sandboxes with high safety levels and
ensure that the competences to support the safe and efficient market entry of innovative technologies are
shared among the regulatory authorities.
Over the recent years EASA has expanded its R&I activities through utilisation of delegated EU funds under
the Horizon Europe Research & Innovation programme, (m 37 s j s l 30M€
addressing a broad set of key domains such as
ꟷ Safety: Lessons learned from accidents, runway safety, digital transformation and new technology
integration.
ꟷ Environment: Emissions and noise standards and non-CO2 emission studies.
ꟷ Health: Aeromedical standards.
ꟷ Security: Assessing the impact of security threats on safety).

3.6. State, Institutional & Military Partnerships
T ’s l l x s d dramatically over the last decade. The repercussions of which
have reshuffled key priorities for citizens, policy makers and the industry alike. The stronger focus on climate
change, environmental protection and sustainability as well as a managing a more complex and challenging
security environment with growing conventional risks as well as the emergence of new threats, such as hybrid
attacks and cyber-attacks.
The development and procurement of not only military aircraft but also state aircraft such as maritime
surveillance assets, fire-fighters, medevac aircraft and mainly drones are increasing and with it the potential for
dual-use cases. Civil-Military dual-use aircraft are designed or adapted to serve both civilian and military
purposes and can operate in commercial aviation, cargo, humanitarian missions or defence roles, creating
opportunities for more efficiency, flexibility, and resilience by bridging civilian and military aviation needs.
As a result, Civil-Military Cooperation (CMC) in the Aviation Sector is increasingly important to enhance safety
and security through coordinated approaches, facilitate sharing or information, expertise and resources,
increase efficiency through harmonisation, simplification and integration of new technologies as well as better
preparedness to respond to emerging threats and challenges, such as climate change, migration, and
cybersecurity threats. The EC has also launched an Action Plan on Military Mobility 2.0 to address the

3.7. Artificial Intelligence
The aviation industry has always been at the forefront of technological innovation, constantly pushing the
boundaries to make air transport safer, more efficient and more accessible. A recent evolution is the rise of
artificial intelligence (AI) and its potential to transform the world of aviation. AI allows us to create systems
that can provide advanced assistance solutions to human end users, optimise aircraft performance, improve
air traffic management and in turn enhance safety in ways that were previously unimaginable.
The deployment of AI in aviation also poses new challenges. As a regulator EASA must ensure that the
European aviation industry can benefit from the potential of AI, in line with EU Regulation 2024/1689 (EU AI
Act), whilst also maintaining the highest standards of safety, security and environmental protection.
Over the last 5 years EASA collaborated with a range of stakeholders in the aviation industry to publish:
ꟷ Two AI concept papers which have paved the way for the approval and deployment of safety-related
AI systems for end-user support (pilots, ATCOs, etc.) and are already being applied to certification
projects through special conditions. These papers were based on the public reports from several
Innovation Partnership Contracts (IPCs) conducted with industry stakeholders, as well as on research
activities on the approval of Machine Learning (ML) technology for systems intended for use in safety-
related applications.
ꟷ The AI Roadmap 2.0 l S ’s vision for addressing the challenges and opportunities of AI in
aviation, intended to serve as a basis for continued discussion with the Agency stakeholders and
subsequent publication of a revised Roadmap 3.0 in the coming years.
Further information can be found on EASA’s website: AI Roadmap | EASA (europa.eu)
Key Developments
INNOVATIVE
‐ Transitioning from AI trustworthiness guidelines into certification and approval
requirements for AI-driven automation.
‐ Integrating the ethical dimension of AI (transparency, non-discrimination,
#Removing obstacles to fairness, etc.) into oversight processes and establishing public confidence in AI-
new technologies enabled aviation products.
‐ Expanding the processes, methods and standards to encompass newest AI
technology and unlock the potential of AI to further improve the current level of
air transport safety.

VI. Environment Management
In 2020 the Agency adopted a comprehensive Sustainable Aviation Programme. The Agency is monitoring and
managing EASA environmental footprint with the following main considerations/actions:
ꟷ Building: Since 2016 we moved to a certified building DGNB gold (German Sustainable
Building Council), with technical features such as: Well water cooling, centralized
ventilation with heat recovery; CAT 2+ certified Data Centre with app. 85% non-active
cooling; LED lights in conference areas; E-chargers for cars and e-bikes.
ꟷ Utilities: The building, located at the main Cologne public transportation hub, optimises the use of
energy and water consumption, and has centralized waste collection points for paper, plastic, residual
waste and glass in the team spaces. We purchase 100% renewable energy. Electrical energy is 100%
renewable (RheinEnergie Ökostrom), while heating energy used is efficient district heating
(Fernwärme), which is produced using 100% fossil resources (natural gas and oil).
ꟷ Supplies: We implemented the Green Public Procurement (GPP) tool for the selection
of contractors such as those for Canteen and Conference Catering services (see below).
In addition, the Sustainable Public Procurement Helpdesk for EU-Institutions and -
Bodies is implemented through inter-institutional FWCs (2025-2029) to support on
GGPs criteria (tender + evaluations). We have reduced paper and office supplies consumption, save
paper/toner/resources with the centralised copy/printing machines, collect used batteries for
recycling, provide paper towels made of recycled paper and install soap and towel dispensers with
sensors all over the building to save cleaning products and resources (water, energy).
ꟷ Services: We included energy management as a service in the tender specifications of
the technical facility management services to ensure optimised operation of EASA
equipment. T s m s v s l d d l dl d’s l

ꟷ Canteen & Conference Catering: The new Canteen & Conference catering provider has
a strong focus on fresh/on-demand cooking, with an emphasis on regional & bio products, reusing
packaging, avoiding single-use plastics, and recycling leftover food into biogas.
ꟷ Transportation: EASA encourages cycling and the use of public transport by providing a reduced

Internal Control Standards
The internal control standards of the Agency are based upon best international practices and on the Internal
Control Framework laid down by the Commission consisting of five internal control components and the
international quality standards (ISO 9001) res l S ’s M m S d ds.

base its activities on the following pillars:
• Leadership – The Agency promotes leadership to establish unity of purpose and direction, maintaining
an environment in which Agency staff can become fully involved in v ’s bj v s
and to proactively manage significant changes.
• Process approach – The Agency adopts a holistic, systemic approach to managing its processes. The
Agency establishes both business and safety objectives and monitors accordingly the performance of
the Integrated Management System and its processes through measurable and agreed performance
indicators, with the view of delivering high quality services ensuring high safety level.
• Continual improvement –The Agency seeks for continual improvement of the Integrated Management

the implementation of a non-punitive internal reporting system where constructive reporting of
business irregularities and safety related issues and concerns is strongly encouraged.

• Efficiency – The Agency seeks to secure sufficient and appropriate available resources and makes the
most efficient use of them through a business, environmental and safety risk-based prioritisation, in
order to offer the most effective and performant services.
• Risk management – The Agency commits to integrating risk management and factual approach into
its decision-making processes. The Agency ensures that its business, environmental and safety risks
are identified, assessed, and managed both at organisation and process level, without compromising
compliance with the applicable regulatory framework. The Agency identifies external and internal
changes that may have an adverse effect on the achievement of its objectives and manages related
risks.
• Safety culture: The Agency recognises the importance of a sound safety culture, including knowledge,
skills, abilities, and motivation for safety management, based on a collective commitment by managers
and staff to emphasize safety over competing goals.
• Relationship with stakeholders – The Agency commits to establish a feedback system that allows the
identification of its internal and external stakeholder expectations and satisfaction level, with the aim
to better meet these expectations, without compromising aviation safety (including when safety
related).
• Internal staff - The Agency seeks to enhance awareness, responsibility, and competences of all staff
with regards to its safety, environmental protection, and quality objectives. The Agency seeks to create
the working environment and culture for the staff to achieve high levels of commitment, motivation,
personal development of competences and satisfaction at the workplace.

• A robust internal audit capability.
• Ex-post and ex-ante controls, exceptions, and delegations of power.

XII. Strategy for Cooperation with Foreign Authorities &
International Organisations
The EU aims to remain a leading global actor in civil aviation, shaping international standards, advancing
sustainability and ensuring high levels of safety worldwide. EASA is central to this ambition, acting as the
technical arm of the EU in international aviation cooperation. Through its activities, the Agency helps ensure
s v l z s, m s d s s s b d, d s s ’s b d
policy priorities such as the Green Deal and Global Gateway.
Mandate and Role
The European legislator has mandated EASA to work with international partners and organisations to enhance
safety and sustainability, to ensure a global level playing field for European industry, and to support Member
States in fulfilling their obligations under the Chicago Convention. By engaging internationally, the Agency
helps project European policy and standards.
Agreements with International Partners
EASA concludes Working Arrangements (WAs) and other cooperation agreements with foreign civil aviation
authorities. More than 150 such agreements have been signed with over 45 States, covering areas such as
certification, safety oversight and acceptance of European products and services. These agreements reduce
duplication, facilitate trade and create market opportunities for EU operators. In the years ahead, EASA will
deepen its relations with key partners, expand cooperation into new areas such as sustainability and
innovation, and pursue additional agreements.
The Agency also supports the European Commission in negotiating and implementing Bilateral Aviation Safety
Agreements (BASAs) and related implementing procedures. Current BASAs with the United States, Canada,
Brazil, China, Japan and the United Kingdom already reduce costs, increase market access and enhance
passenger confidence. Future negotiations with other major aviation partners will extend these benefits
further.
Cooperation with International Organisations
EASA maintains a close working relationship with the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO), providing
technical expertise, exchanging safety data through the EASA–ICAO Working Arrangement, and helping
coordinate common European positions. The Agency plays a key role in implementing ICAO standards,
including climate-related measures such as CORSIA and the Long-Term Aspirational Goal (LTAG).
